description: Four-panel composite figure reporting tensile behaviour of ultrafast-cooled Fe-20Mn-9Al-1.5C steels with Ni and Cr additions. (a) Engineering stress (MPa, 0-1400, 200 ticks) vs engineering strain (0-0.6) with the legend 3Cr (black), 2Ni (red), 2Ni3Cr (blue), 2Ni5Cr (green). The red 2Ni curve rises steeply to the highest peak, just above the 1200 MPa gridline, then declines and terminates near strain 0.33; blue 2Ni3Cr ends near 0.42, green 2Ni5Cr near 0.50, and black 3Cr extends furthest, to ~0.55, after a lower, flatter plateau near 1100 MPa. (b) True stress (MPa, 0-1800) vs true strain (0-0.6), same colour code; curves cross, with 2Ni5Cr and 3Cr reaching the highest stresses, near the 1600-1800 MPa band, at the largest strains. (c) Strain hardening rate (MPa, 0-3000, 500 ticks) vs true strain, with hollow circles and Roman numerals marking three hardening stages I, II and III; 3Cr and 2Ni5Cr give the highest stage-II plateaus (near 2000 MPa), while 2Ni falls abruptly to zero near true strain 0.25. (d) Yield strength YS (MPa, 0-1600) vs TS x TEL (GPa-%), 0-80, comparing literature Fe-Al, Fe-Mn, Fe-Mn-C, Fe-Mn-Al-C, 301LN and 304 stainless steels with the present steels (red stars), which lie in an otherwise empty upper-right region above a shaded boundary. Together the panels argue that Ni+Cr alloying breaks the strength-ductility trade-off.

observations.observation: Panel (a) legend identifies the four colour-coded alloys exactly as 3Cr (black), 2Ni (red), 2Ni3Cr (blue) and 2Ni5Cr (green).
Panel (a) axes are Engineering stress (MPa) from 0 to 1400 with ticks every 200, and Engineering strain from 0.0 to 0.6 with ticks every 0.1; no numeric data labels are printed on the curves.

In panel (a) the red 2Ni curve reaches the highest engineering stress, peaking just above the 1200 MPa gridline at small strain, and is the first to terminate, at an engineering strain of roughly 0.33-0.35.
In panel (a) the black 3Cr curve is the lowest-strength but extends furthest, terminating between the 0.5 and 0.6 strain gridlines, while green 2Ni5Cr terminates near 0.5 and blue 2Ni3Cr near 0.42.

Panel (b) plots True stress (MPa, 0-1800) against True strain (0-0.6) with the same four-colour legend; the curves cross, and 2Ni5Cr (green) and 3Cr (black) reach the highest true stresses at the largest strains.
Panel (c) plots Strain hardening rate (MPa, 0-3000) against True strain (0-0.6) and marks three strain-hardening stages with Roman numerals I, II and III and hollow circles at the stage boundaries.
In panel (c) the red 2Ni curve falls to zero strain hardening rate near true strain 0.25, earlier than the blue 2Ni3Cr (~0.35) and the green 2Ni5Cr and black 3Cr curves.
Panel (d) x-axis is TS x TEL in GPa-% (0-80, ticks every 10) and y-axis is YS in MPa (0-1600, ticks every 200).

Panel (d) legend distinguishes literature data by symbol - Fe-Al steel, Fe-Mn steel, Fe-Mn-C steel, Fe-Mn-Al-C steel, 301LN stainless steel, 304 stainless steel - from the red stars labelled 'this study'.

In panel (d) the red stars of 'this study' occupy an empty upper-right region above a light-blue shaded boundary, sitting between the 1000 and 1200 MPa YS gridlines and between about 45 and 70 GPa-% on the TS x TEL axis.

The caption states the figure compares tensile properties of 3Cr, 2Ni, 2Ni3Cr and 2Ni5Cr steel, with panels (a) engineering stress-strain, (b) true stress-strain, (c) strain hardening curves and (d) TS x TEL versus tensile strength.

The caption states the literature data in (d) come from Fe-Al [42], Fe-Mn [43,44], Fe-Mn-C [45,46,47], Fe-Mn-Al-C [14,36,45,46,48] and stainless steels [49,50], and that the raw tensile data are given in Table 2.
The citing text states the yield and tensile strengths of 2Ni steel are 1202 MPa and 1283 MPa, and those of 3Cr steel (no added Ni) are 969 MPa and 1141 MPa.
The citing text states that relative to 3Cr steel, the higher-Ni 2Ni3Cr steel has a yield strength increase of ~141 MPa, and that the total elongation of 2Ni5Cr is ~16% higher than that of 2Ni steel.

The citing text describes two families of work-hardening curves in (c): black/green (3Cr and 2Ni5Cr) and blue/red (2Ni and 2Ni3Cr), and states that stage II is prolonged with increasing Cr content while increasing Ni shortens and lowers stages II and III.

subfigures.description: Engineering stress (MPa, 0-1400) vs engineering strain (0-0.6) for four colour-coded curves: 3Cr (black), 2Ni (red), 2Ni3Cr (blue), 2Ni5Cr (green). 2Ni gives the highest peak stress but the shortest elongation; 3Cr gives the longest elongation with a lower flow stress. No numeric data labels are printed.

True stress (MPa, 0-1800) vs true strain (0-0.6) for the same four alloys and colour code. The curves cross; 2Ni terminates earliest (~0.25 true strain), while 2Ni5Cr and 3Cr reach the highest true stresses at the largest strains.

Strain hardening rate (MPa, 0-3000) vs true strain (0-0.6). Hollow circles mark boundaries between three hardening stages labelled I, II and III. All four steels show a sharp initial drop (stage I), a rise/plateau (stage II) near 1500-2100 MPa, then a decline to zero (stage III); the 2Ni red curve drops to zero near 0.25 true strain, earliest of the four.

Scatter plot of yield strength YS (MPa, 0-1600) vs TS x TEL (GPa-%), 0-80, with legend entries Fe-Al steel, Fe-Mn steel, Fe-Mn-C steel, Fe-Mn-Al-C steel, 301LN stainless steel, 304 stainless steel and 'this study' (red stars). The present steels (red stars) sit in the upper-right area at high TS x TEL and YS between ~1000 and 1150 MPa, above a light-blue shaded boundary outlining the literature data.

unreadable_items: panel (a): no numeric values are printed on the curves, so peak stresses and fracture strains can only be located relative to axis gridlines
panel (c): stage-boundary hollow circles carry no printed coordinates; the stage I/II/III transition strains are not labelled numerically
panel (d): individual literature and 'this study' data points carry no printed coordinates and no clearly resolvable error bars
